Where it began

Waqar Younis was born in Burewala, in the Punjab, on 16 November 1971, but he spent his boyhood in Sharjah, where his father had found work. He came back to Pakistan as a teenager and threw himself into sport of every kind: he ran, threw the javelin, high-jumped and tried the pole vault. On the cricket field he started out bowling leg-spin before deciding that running in fast was more his style.

He had played only six first-class matches when his chance came. Imran Khan watched him bowl on television, turned up at the ground to see the end of the game, and the next day told the young man he would be going to Sharjah with Pakistan. For someone who had grown up there, it was a fitting first trip.

The player

His Test debut, against India in November 1989, fell on his eighteenth birthday and was also the first Test of a certain Sachin Tendulkar. Waqar took four wickets, Tendulkar and Kapil Dev among them. Over 87 Tests, up to 2003, he took 373 wickets at 23.56, with 22 five-wicket innings, five ten-wicket matches and a best of 7 for 76. When this profile was written, only 22 men had taken more.

In his first 29 Tests he took 170 wickets, and for a few years at the start of the 1990s he was thought the fastest bowler in the world. He captained Pakistan in 17 Tests and won ten of them, and when he first took charge, at 22, he became the youngest man ever to lead Pakistan in a Test. For Surrey in 1991 he took 113 first-class wickets at 14.65 and topped the national averages, and in 1997 he helped Glamorgan win the County Championship, taking 7 for 25 with a hat-trick against Lancashire at Liverpool.

What made him special

Pace, and what he did with it. Waqar could make an old ball swing the wrong way, late and very fast, so batters who had judged the line found the ball heading somewhere else entirely. With Wasim Akram at the other end, Pakistan had an opening pair that no batting side looked forward to facing.

He went for wickets rather than maidens, so an off day could cost a few runs, a fair price for the good days. His batting was gentler. He made 1,010 Test runs with a highest score of 45, which means he walked out to bat 120 times without once raising his bat for fifty. Few people can claim that kind of patience.

Away from the middle

The cricket world called him Wiki, or the Burewala Express. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1992, received Pakistan's Pride of Performance award and was inducted into the ICC Hall of Fame in 2013. After playing he coached Pakistan, both as head coach and as bowling coach and spent time behind the microphone as a television commentator. Lasith Malinga said he learned his yorker by watching Waqar and Wasim.

And finally

As a small boy in Jamaica, Usain Bolt bowled a bit himself and supported Pakistan, largely because of Waqar. It seems right that the fastest man on the track should have started out cheering for one of the fastest men with a cricket ball.
